name: Maya Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Maya. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is ever tied to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm with the council's home care team on the east side, so my day starts at seven with Mr Hollis on Station Road, who needs help getting washed and dressed. Then it's breakfasts, tablets, a couple of hoist transfers with another carer, and lunches around half eleven. I've only been doing this two years and I'm still slow with the hoist paperwork and the medicine charts, honestly. What I like is the talking, the people who wait by the window for you. What wears me out is the rota changing every week and the phone app we're meant to log every visit on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned the app. Tell me a bit more about that, and about life outside work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The app is meant to track our times and our notes, and I hate it, I'll be honest. I still write my notes on paper in the folder at each house and then type the bare minimum, and my team leader Denise keeps on at me about it. At home it's me and my partner Tomás, he drives the number 14 bus, and we've no kids yet. My nan left me a share of her flat, which we rent out, so we've a bit put by, more than most carers I know. The council pays better than the private agencies, and that's partly because we're in the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, frankly. Every year someone tells us a gadget is going to fix care, and every year it's still two women and a hoist at seven in the morning. At work I'd just say it was a lot of noise about nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, but I'd still be worried about the council's money. Budgets get cut whether AI happens or not, and they're always looking at shortening visits from thirty minutes to fifteen. If the app gets a bit smarter, they'll use it to time us even closer. That's my real worry, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my round and keep going to the union branch meetings on the first Tuesday. I'd keep putting money aside from the flat rent like we do now, about two hundred a month. And I'd probably still refuse to use the voice notes thing they keep pushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. I like knowing what I'm doing tomorrow. There's a bit of tiredness about the same old fights over visit times, but nothing new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the app gets used to time you closer. Has that already happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, last spring. They looked at the logged times and said our tea visits ran over, so now they're down to twenty minutes. You can't make a cup of tea, help someone to the toilet and ask how their week was in twenty minutes. Denise fought it, but the managers had the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about that, outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomás mostly, because he gets the same thing on the buses with the timing screens. We moan about it over dinner. My mum thinks I should go into nursing, but I left school at fifteen and I'm not going back to a classroom.

say: I'd tell people the **AI hype** was noise and care is still two carers and a **hoist** at seven.
I'd say the real fight is about **visit times**, not gadgets.
think: Privately I'm **relieved**, but council **budget cuts** worry me more than any robot.
A smarter app would just be used to **time us** even closer.
do: Keep my **round** and attend the union **branch meetings** every first Tuesday.
Save about **two hundred** a month from the rented flat.
Keep **refusing** the voice notes feature and writing notes on paper.
feel: Settled and **steady**, with some tiredness about the old **fights** over visit times.
S0.quote: You can't make a cup of tea, help someone to the toilet and ask how their week was in twenty minutes.
fieldNote: Her pressure comes from **council budgets** and timed visits, not from AI.
She is strongly **union-minded** and blames managers' numbers rather than technology itself.
The rented share of her nan's **flat** gives her a cushion most carers lack.

steps.text: Keep the morning round on Station Road with the council team
Attend the union branch meeting every first Tuesday
Put two hundred a month from the flat rent into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: the AI will do the office work and they'll use it as an excuse to cut corners on us. If it's planning the rota and writing the care plans, fine, but someone has to check it. I'd probably post that on the union group too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, I think my hands-on bit is safe for a while, because no robot is getting Mrs Adeyemi in and out of the bath any time soon. But the planning will be done by a computer that's never met her. I'm bad with the tech, and if everything goes through the app I'll be the one who's always getting it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a say on how the rota software is used, like no visits under thirty minutes whatever the computer says. I'd keep saving. I'd probably ask Tomás to sit with me and show me the app properly, though I'd still avoid it where I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, really. Not scared for my job, but annoyed, and worried I'll fall behind the younger ones who just tap through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd fall behind. What does falling behind look like in your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's getting called into the office for missed logs. I've had two warnings already for notes not being typed in by the end of the shift. If the computer plans everything, my handwritten notes in the blue folder become a problem instead of the proper record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Denise, my team leader, because half her job is the rota and the phone calls. If a program does that, they might not need a team leader per patch. And the coordinators in the office, they're lovely and they'd be first to go.

say: I'd say AI will do the **office work** and managers will use it to **cut corners**.
I'd post on the **union group** that someone human must check every rota.
think: My **hands-on** care feels safe for now, because baths and hoists need people.
I'm bad with **tech**, so an app-run job could make me the one getting **warnings**.
do: Push the **union** to set a thirty-minute **minimum** that rota software can't override.
Ask Tomás to teach me the **app** properly, while still avoiding it where I can.
Keep **saving** the flat rent each month.
feel: **Uneasy** and annoyed rather than afraid for my **job**.
Worried about **falling behind** younger carers who handle the app easily.
S1.quote: If the computer plans everything, my handwritten notes in the blue folder become a problem instead of the proper record.
fieldNote: She sees a clear split: **office tasks** go first, her hands-on work stays.
Her fear is **discipline** over missed logs, not redundancy.
She worries for **Denise** and office coordinators more than for herself.

steps.text: Push the union for a thirty-minute visit minimum the software can't cut
Keep saving the flat rent every month
Keep doing hoist and bath visits on the east side

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a scandal that nobody prepared. I'd be saying the government should have rules before any robot goes into an old person's home. I'd be at the protest if there was one, with my union lanyard on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, two years is nothing, and three years after that is 2031, when I'd be thirty-two. The paperwork and the rota go straight away, and then the robots come for the washing and dressing. The council will buy whatever's cheapest the minute it's allowed. I've no qualifications and I don't use any of this tech, so I'd be first in the queue when the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd get more involved with the union, maybe become a rep, because that's where the decisions get fought. I'd stop spending on holidays and keep every penny of the flat rent. Tomás and I would talk seriously about whether he's safe on the buses, because driverless buses might come even sooner. I'd probably start looking at what jobs still need a person in a room, like day centres.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightening, to be truthful. My stomach turns thinking about it. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do sums. What do the sums say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between the flat and our savings we could last over a year, maybe two if we were careful. But if both of us lose our jobs in the same few years, that runs out. And there'd be thousands of carers all looking at once, so 'plenty of jobs nearby' wouldn't mean much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mr Hollis about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't, at first. He'd get upset. Maybe I'd tell him I'm fighting to make sure he still gets a real person, because he would want one. He told me once he'd rather go into a home than have a machine wipe him.

say: I'd call it a **scandal** that nobody prepared and demand **rules** before robots enter homes.
I'd turn up to any **protest** wearing my union lanyard.
think: Two years for AGI and robots by **2031** leaves me only five years in care.
With **no qualifications** and no tech habits, I'd be **first** out.
do: Stand to become a union **rep** within the first year.
Cut **holidays** and save all of the **flat rent**.
Look at **day centre** jobs that still need a person in the room.
feel: **Frightened**, with a turning stomach and **sleepless** nights doing sums.
S2.quote: I've no qualifications and I don't use any of this tech, so I'd be first in the queue when the robots come.
fieldNote: The **double risk** of her and Tomás losing work in the same years drives her fear.
Her savings feel real but **not enough** if thousands of carers job hunt at once.
She answers with **collective action** first, not with learning new skills.

steps.text: Stand as a union rep for the east side care team
Back campaigns for rules before robots go into older people's homes
Cancel this year's holiday and bank all of the flat rent
Look for day centre jobs that still need people in the room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really, that we need rules and the union at the table. But with five years I'd say it more calmly. I'd say this is the moment to write the rules, while there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years plus three for robots puts it at 2034, when I'm thirty-five. That's long enough that I could maybe change direction, but I know myself and I'd keep putting it off. The office side would go in 2031 and I think Denise and the coordinators would be gone then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to get on a union training course about bargaining over technology, they do those. I might look at the day centre in Elm Park, because group care with lots of people in one room seems harder for a robot. I'd keep saving and maybe pay off the little bit left on our car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but I can breathe. It's more of a heavy feeling than a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep putting it off. What would make you actually do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably someone I know going first. If Rosa from my team moved to the day centre and liked it, I'd follow her. I'm not brave about change, I need to see someone I trust do it before I go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut if money gets tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out, and the gym I never go to. We'd keep the flat rented out, that's our safety. I wouldn't touch the savings unless we had to.

say: I'd say we need **rules** and the union at the table, and five years is time to **write them**.
I'd sound **calmer** than in the fast version.
think: Robots by **2034** gives me room to change, but I'd **put it off**.
The **office side** would go in 2031, taking Denise's job.
do: Join a union **training course** on bargaining over new technology.
Look at the **day centre** in Elm Park as a next step.
Pay off the **car** and keep saving the rent.
feel: A **heavy** worry rather than panic, with room to **breathe**.
S3.quote: I'm not brave about change, I need to see someone I trust do it before I go.
fieldNote: She knows she **delays change** and needs a trusted colleague to go first.
Five years turns her **anger** into planning, but her own job still looks likely to shrink.
The rented flat is her **safety line** and she won't touch it.

steps.text: Sign up for the union course on bargaining over technology
Visit the Elm Park day centre and ask about openings
Pay off the car and keep the rent in savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it properly, with care workers having a say. I'd tell people not to let the companies use the time just to get ready to sack us. I'd keep saying it at branch meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be thirty-seven when the robots come, in 2039. That's still young enough to start something else but old enough to be tired. I'd like to think I'd train for something, but I'm being honest that I'd probably just carry on until it's on top of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in my job, keep saving, and keep pushing the union on rules. Maybe in a few years I'd try a short course, something like activities coordinator, which is still people. Tomás and I would maybe decide on kids, because ten years feels like enough room to have them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but a bit uneasy underneath. Ten years is a long time and anything can happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. Would this change that decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might make it easier, weirdly. With two years I'd say no way. With ten years before the robots come, I'd feel I could have a baby and still sort out the job after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably carry on till it's on top of you. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes. My mum would say I always leave things to the last minute, and she's right. But I've got the flat behind me, so I'd have time to sort myself out even if I'm late.

say: I'd say ten years is enough to do it **properly**, with care workers given a **say**.
I'd warn that firms shouldn't use the time just to plan **layoffs**.
think: At **thirty-seven** in 2039, I could still start something new.
I'd probably **carry on** until the change is right on top of me.
do: Stay in my **council job** and keep saving every month.
Try a short **activities coordinator** course in a few years.
Talk with Tomás about having **children** sooner.
feel: **Calmer** overall, but **uneasy** underneath because a decade is unpredictable.
S4.quote: With ten years before the robots come, I'd feel I could have a baby and still sort out the job after.
fieldNote: Ten years shifts her focus to **family plans**, not career moves.
She openly admits she **leaves things late** and leans on her cushion.
Her outlook stays **union-first** across all three AGI timelines.

steps.text: Stay on the council home care team and keep saving
Keep raising technology rules at union branch meetings
Plan with Tomás whether to have a baby in the next few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. Two years for the computers and five for the robots, and I've no qualifications and no tech. What would help is the union having a proper say on robots in care, and paid retraining that doesn't feel like going back to school.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what the old people want. Nobody ever asks them. My client Mr Hollis would rather be lifted by a tired carer who knows his name than by a perfect machine that doesn't.

headlineQuote: My client Mr Hollis would rather be lifted by a tired carer who knows his name than by a perfect machine that doesn't.
portrait: Maya is a **27-year-old** council home carer, two years in, still slow with paperwork and the visit app.
She is a committed **union member** who blames budgets and managers, not technology itself.
The rented share of her nan's **flat** gives her and Tomás a cushion most carers lack.
She stays calm in the slow pictures but becomes **alarmed** when AGI comes by 2028.
She admits she **delays change** and would follow a trusted colleague rather than lead.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots by 2031 would hit her with no qualifications or tech skills.
whatWouldHelp: A proper **union say** on robots in care.
**Paid retraining** that doesn't feel like going back to school.
